think:
1. Core Clinical Tension: A 27-year-old Indonesian male presents with recurrent, itchy erythematous-to-brown plaques and acute bullous, edematous eruptions on his right lower extremity associated with profound peripheral hypereosinophilia (57%, WBC 19,300/uL), constitutional symptoms, diarrhea, and a 7 kg weight loss. The clinical dilemma lies in distinguishing an idiopathic clonal or reactive hypereosinophilic syndrome or primary eosinophilic cellulitis (Wells' syndrome) from an underlying helminthic infestation, compounded by secondary bacterial infection of the cutaneous blisters.
2. Admission Breakpoint: The admission breakpoint occurs following physical examination of the skin lesions, routine triage laboratory testing demonstrating leukocytosis with profound eosinophilia, and direct Gram stain of bulla fluid, prior to punch skin biopsy histopathology, specialized stool culture for larvae, and helminthic serology.
3. Differential Distinctions: Idiopathic hypereosinophilic syndrome or primary Wells' syndrome was considered because of the marked peripheral eosinophilia and typical recurrent dermal plaques with classic flame figures, but this inflammatory state was triggered secondarily by helminthic parasites. Primary acute bacterial cellulitis or bullous impetigo was considered due to Gram-positive cocci on fluid microscopy, but bacterial growth was a superficial superinfection on pre-existing eosinophilic dermatosis. Diagnosis of soil-transmitted helminthiasis was established by identification of Strongyloides stercoralis larvae and positive Toxocara serology.
case_prompt:
A 27-year-old man presents to the dermatology clinic in Bandung, Indonesia, with severe pruritus, blister formation, and worsening cutaneous edema overlying recurrent brownish-red lesions on his right lower leg, accompanied by fever and acute watery diarrhea that began five days ago.

The patient's dermatologic symptoms began six months earlier as an itchy, nummular erythematous macule that expanded into a plaque and evolved into a brownish lesion, which transiently subsided into hyperpigmentation following topical therapy. One month later, he experienced systemic symptoms consisting of fever, rigors, arthralgias, and cephalalgia that resolved with antipyretics and antihistamines, after which similar pruritic plaques recurred in the same anatomical distribution. Three months prior to presentation, he developed recurrent fevers, crampy abdominal pain, and chronic diarrhea accompanied by an unintentional weight loss of 7 kilograms. Epidemiological history is notable for regular consumption of unwashed raw vegetables and ownership of a domestic cat.

On physical examination, prominent non-pitting cutaneous edema is noted on the right lower leg with multiple brownish erythematous plaques measuring up to 10 x 6 cm without local warmth or induration. Surrounding these plaques are numerous tense bullae and crusted lesions ranging from 0.5 x 0.5 cm to 1.2 x 1.2 cm in dimension.

Triage complete blood count demonstrates leukocytosis with a white blood cell count of 19,300/uL and profound peripheral eosinophilia accounting for 57% of differential leukocytes. Direct Gram stain of fluid aspirated from hypopyon bullae reveals abundant polymorphonuclear leukocytes (>10/high-power field) and Gram-positive cocci.

diagnostic_reasoning.candidate: Primary Idiopathic Wells' Syndrome (Eosinophilic Cellulitis) / Primary Hypereosinophilic Syndrome
diagnostic_reasoning.rule_out_reason: Considered due to the recurrent cutaneous plaques, profound peripheral eosinophilia (57%), and dermal eosinophilic infiltration displaying flame figures, but ruled out as an idiopathic primary disorder because the hypereosinophilia and reactive cutaneous eruption were driven by underlying parasitic infestation.
diagnostic_reasoning.quote: Histopathological features revealed no alterations to the epidermis, but there was extensive infiltration of eosinophilic inflammatory cells from the dermal papillae to the subcutaneous fat layer... some displaying flame figures, indicating Wells' syndrome... A peripheral blood smear was conducted and showed leukocytosis (19.300/uL) with a significant predominance of eosinophils (57%).

diagnostic_reasoning.rule_out_reason: Considered due to acute inflammatory bullae and the presence of Gram-positive cocci on fluid examination, but the bacterial findings represented secondary bacterial impetiginization over an underlying eosinophilic dermatosis.
diagnostic_reasoning.quote: Direct microscopic examination of hypopyon bullae fluid using Gram staining revealed a large number of polymorphonuclear (PMN) leukocytes (PMN > 10/large view) and the presence of Gram-positive cocci bacteria... The patient received a diagnosis of Wells' syndrome with secondary infection

diagnostic_reasoning.rule_out_reason: Isolation of Strongyloides stercoralis larvae on stool culture together with positive Toxocara IgG serology (index 2.04) confirmed soil-transmitted helminthiasis as the underlying etiology driving hypereosinophilia and reactive Wells' syndrome, which resolved upon treatment with albendazole.
diagnostic_reasoning.quote: Strongyloidiasis was confirmed by the identification of S. stercoralis in a stool culture (Figure 3). The Toxocara immunoglobulin G (IgG) antibody was assessed using the hydatid cyst serology assay method... The result was positive, with an index of 2.04. The patient received a diagnosis of Wells' syndrome with secondary infection and concurrent strongyloidiasis and toxocariasis.

editor_comments: Strict admission breakpoint preserved prior to biopsy and stool parasitology. Presentation free of pathogen spoilers.
